newsitem.title: USA: Talk of Brazil soy exports to U.S. persists.
newsitem.headline: Talk of Brazil soy exports to U.S. persists.

text.p: Rumors that U.S. soybean crushers and livestock producers are still considering importing soybeans or soymeal from Brazil continued to circulate in U.S. markets, traders said.
"Yes, there are more processors looking to bring beans in from South America," said one U.S. soymeal exporter.
In addition to talk that U.S. soybean crushers will import more soybeans from Brazil, talk that California livestock producers were seeking to import soymeal have also surfaced.
U.S. traders and exporters couldn't confirm any trades, however.
"We've been looking at that trade for the past three or four months," said a feed dealer from northern California. "If my operation were big enough, I'd be doing it."
The dealer said that prices were favorable for importing soymeal to California, but it was profitable only in quantities of 15,000 to 20,000 tonnes.
"Whenever prices get low enough in South America, the possibility for imports tends to be California or the Southeast--wherever you're near a port," said the U.S. exporter.
Basis values in Brazil for soymeal pellets FOB Paranagua have fallen $3.00 per tonne since Monday, while basis values for soybeans have climbed five cents per bushel.
Sourcing soybeans out of South America remains attractive because prices there still hold a substantial discount to those in the U.S., traders and exporters said.
One southeastern U.S. soymeal dealer said he doubted talk of Brazilian soymeal exports to California because of expenses associated with reprocessing the feed for poultry.
If the meal were used for chicken feed, it would have to be ground further so nutrients could be added, he said.
But dairy cows could consume the feed without it being reprocessed and California has a large dairy cow herd, other dealers said.
"They (California producers) are used to feeding more flexible items," said the soymeal exporter. "A cow has a stomach like a washing machine."

Earlier this month, commodities giant Cargill Inc announced that they had contracted to import soybeans from Brazil. This spring, Owensboro Grain, a soybean crusher in Kentucky, confirmed the purchase of soybeans from Brazil.
In response to the Cargill announcement, July soybeans closed down the 30-cent per bushel daily trading limit.
